mechanisms.name: /usr/bin/sandbox-exec
mechanisms.note: shipped and functional on this host, but it is a thin wrapper over sandbox_init, which <sandbox.h> declares deprecated. Apple publishes no replacement for applying a dynamic profile to an arbitrary already-built binary.

mechanisms.name: sandbox_init / sandbox_init_with_parameters (libsystem_sandbox)
mechanisms.note: declared deprecated in the public SDK header. The named built-in profiles it accepts are coarse; a per-operation profile requires the profile language below.

mechanisms.name: seatbelt profile language (version 1 S-expressions)
mechanisms.note: not a published, versioned interface. Operation names and filter semantics are discovered from the shipped profiles under /usr/share/sandbox and can change between releases without notice.

mechanisms.name: App Sandbox (com.apple.security.app-sandbox entitlement)
mechanisms.note: supported and non-deprecated, but it applies to a signed, entitled bundle. It cannot be imposed on an arbitrary toolchain binary the manager did not build and sign, and its container model does not express an exact executable allowlist.

mechanisms.name: Endpoint Security framework
mechanisms.note: an authorization client could veto exec system-wide, but it requires the com.apple.developer.endpoint-security.client entitlement, which Apple grants case by case, plus a system extension and full disk access. It is also a global authorizer, not a per-operation domain.

mechanisms.name: POSIX process group and session
mechanisms.note: the only grouping a plain macOS supervisor can create. A descendant leaves it with setsid, so it is not an unescapable domain.

mechanisms.name: setrlimit RLIMIT_AS / RLIMIT_NOFILE / RLIMIT_NPROC / RLIMIT_CPU
mechanisms.note: per process, inherited by children as a fresh budget each. RLIMIT_NPROC is per user, not per operation. None of them account over a process tree.

mechanisms.name: Mach task ports and task_policy_set
mechanisms.note: task_for_pid on another process requires elevated privilege and is blocked by SIP for protected processes. The policy interfaces set scheduling and QoS bands, not hard aggregate bounds.

mechanisms.name: Linux cgroup v2 equivalent
mechanisms.note: macOS has no cgroup-style controller. There is no pids.max, memory.max or cgroup.kill analogue exposed to third-party code.

mechanisms.name: Windows Job Object equivalent
mechanisms.note: macOS exposes nothing with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE semantics: no kernel object that a descendant cannot leave and whose destruction destroys every member.

mechanisms.name: Filesystem quotas (edquota, quotacheck)
mechanisms.note: per user or group on a whole volume, requires root, and is not enabled on a default APFS install. It cannot bound the bytes one operation writes below one private directory.

mechanisms.name: Disk image (hdiutil) as a size-bounded private volume
mechanisms.note: a fixed-size attached image does bound bytes written below the build root, which is the one aggregate quantity macOS can enforce without private interfaces. It costs an attach and detach per operation and still does not bound memory, processes or CPU.

mechanisms.name: Virtualization.framework guest
mechanisms.note: a guest is an unescapable domain with aggregate memory and CPU bounds and atomic destruction. It is the only public macOS mechanism that satisfies the three blocking classes, at the cost of a guest image in the trusted computing base and a much larger per-operation setup.

mechanisms.name: chroot
mechanisms.note: requires root and is not a security boundary on macOS. It does not remove the global path namespace for a process that can create a new root, and it does not bound anything else.

mechanisms.name: posix_spawn POSIX_SPAWN_START_SUSPENDED plus a pre-exec sandbox call
mechanisms.note: the usual way to apply a profile without sandbox-exec still calls the deprecated sandbox_init in the child. It changes who calls the interface, not whether the interface is deprecated.
